How far will you go to seek glory and fame? Will you risk losing everything? In Dungeon Roll the player's goal is to collect the most experience points by defeating monsters, battling the dragon, and amassing treasure. Each player selects a Hero avatar, such as a Mercenary, Half-Goblin, or Enchantress, which provides them with unique powers. Then players take turns being the Adventurer, who boldly enters the dungeon seeking glory. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Player's Turn 2.1 Monster Phase 2.2 Loot Phase 2.3 Dragon Phase 2.4 Regroup Phase 3 Party Dice 3.1 Companion Types and Special Ability 4 Treasures 5 Hero Powers 5.1 Basic Heroes 5.2 Hero Pack 1 5.3 Promo 5.4 Hero Pack 2 6 End of Game Objective Complete 3 dungeon delves to gain experience and treasure. Fight monsters, slay dragons and attempt to level up. Will you become Hero of the Ages? Player's Turn The adventurer rolls 7 party dice to determine their companions. Dungeon dice are also rolled - one die per level. Dungeon dice can be monsters to defeat, treasures chests to open, potions to drink or dragons. You will gain 1 experience point per level cleared of monsters and/or dragons. You must defeat monsters before your companion dice can open chests or drink potions. Then you must slay the dragon if there are 3 or more dragon dice in the lair. Monster Phase Roll a number of dungeon dice equals to the level (up to 10) as the monsters. Set aside all dragons in the dragon's lair: they cannot be rerolled. The adventurer can use a scroll to reroll any number of party and/or dungeon dice. Tip: To use a scroll or fight monsters, move the party and dungeon dice to the Playing Area. The adventurer uses their companions to fight monsters. Companion dice are moved to the graveyard after use. The adventurer can use their hero's specialty (multiple uses per delve) or their ultimate ability (one use per delve). If the monsters are defeated, proceed to the loot phase. If you can't defeat all of the monsters, the adventurer flees and gains no experience (but keeps any treasure tokens they have). Loot Phase A thief or a champion can open any number of chests. Other companion types can only open one chest. The adventurer gets a treasure for each opened chest. If there are no treasures left, use experience as a replacement. Any party die can quaff any number of potions. A potion can revive a companion with its face chosen by the adventurer, adding companions back into your party for the next round. Dragon Phase When there are 3 or more dragon dice in the lair, the Dragon attacks the adventurer: To defeat the dragon, you must use 3 different types of companions (not scrolls). NOTE: Hero abilities that allow one type of companion to act as another allow two dice showing the same die face to be counted as two different types of companions. If the dragon is not defeated, the adventurer flees and gain no experience (but keeps any treasure tokens). If the dragon is defeated, the adventurer gains a treasure token and 1 experience. Regroup Phase The adventurer can choose between retiring to the tavern and seeking glory: Retire: collect experience points equal to the level just completed. The current delve is over. Seek glory: move on to the next dungeon level with all remaining party dice and treasure tokens. The number of dungeon dice increases by 1 for the new level (Level 1 uses 1 dungeon die, Level 2 uses 2 dungeon dice, etc). After completing Level 10, the adventurer has cleared the entire dungeon and must retire. Party Dice Companion Types and Special Ability ALL companions can: Defeat 1 monster Open 1 treasure chest Quaff any number of potions A mage (blue wizard's hat icon) can defeat any number of oozes. [Rating: 1/10] Meh hype...,sux0rs.  More of a grueling exercise than a game.  Seriously the creator of this teaches us all a lesson in colorful garbage. I'd rather play monopoly or hammer my fingers with it really.  I think I'll use it to punish children since spanking is taboo nowadays.

[Rating: 1/10] the most hideously overhyped piece of stupid garbage since Quarriors.  Nice fonts on the dice.. that's the nicest thing I can say about this horrible game.

[Rating: 1/10] Dissapointed! A shallow game. Played it twice, watched several videos here on BGG to see if I'd played it wrong as it was tremendously boring.  The game _looks_ very good (that's why I bought it), but this product shouldn't have evolved past the PnP it originally was.

[Rating: 1/10] I won this game, so my rating is a little better seeing as I did not pay for it. Absolute garbage.

[Rating: 1/10] A very bad solitaire game pretending to be a horrible multi-player game.  No meaningful game play, only enjoyable by people who get off on rolling dice for no reason.

[Rating: 1/10] Just look at the variants for this game. Out of the box it's an unusually boring design. Sold as soon as I could.

[Rating: 1/10] One of the worst filler "games" I have ever played.  With solo play or 2 player, the pain is lessened because it can be over rather quickly.  But with 3 or 4 players, you will spend quite a bit of time playing with your smart phone.  IMO, games of this weight should either be designed so that turns are quick or present some sort of device where players remain involved when it is not their turn.  This game fails on both of these. And rolling the dungeon dice when it is another player's turn does not count as interaction.  If I am rolling your dungeon dice, I could not care less what is rolled.

[Rating: 1/10] Push your luck dice chucker with obvious decisions and is long.  The core element is simply not that compelling and the fantasy dressing cannot lift it.  Check out Can't Stop, Incan Gold or even Martian Dice instead.

[Rating: 1/10] [b]A dungeon crawl reduced to asking the dice for permission.[/b] Roll a party, roll some monsters, match the appropriate icons, then decide whether to push onward and risk losing the haul. Heroes and treasures decorate the procedure without rescuing it from its central emptiness. The supposed tension comes almost entirely from gambling against another roll rather than from constructing a plan. Fantasy adventure compressed into repetitive probability checks.
